paragraphs.heading: Heat held in
paragraphs.text: The greenhouse effect is the warming of a planet's surface that happens when gases in its atmosphere hold back heat the planet would otherwise lose to space. The heat can come from inside the planet, as with Jupiter, or from outside, such as a host star. On Earth, the Sun's shortwave radiation, which we call sunlight, passes through the greenhouse gases and warms the surface. The surface then gives off longwave radiation, and greenhouse gases absorb most of it, slowing how fast Earth can cool.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of radiation
paragraphs.text: Anything warmer than absolute zero gives off thermal radiation, and the Sun and Earth emit different wavelengths because their temperatures differ. The Sun's surface is 5,500 °C, so most of its energy leaves as shortwave radiation in visible and near-infrared light. Earth's surface is far cooler and emits longwave radiation at mid- and far-infrared wavelengths. A gas counts as a greenhouse gas if it absorbs longwave radiation. Earth's air absorbs only 23% of incoming shortwave radiation but 90% of the longwave radiation from the surface, so energy builds up and the surface warms.

paragraphs.heading: How big the effect is
paragraphs.text: Without this absorption, Earth's surface would average −18 °C (−0.4 °F); with it, the average is around 15 °C (59 °F). So the effect can be measured as a temperature change of 33 °C. It can also be measured in energy: longwave radiation leaves the surface at an average of 398 W/m², yet only 239 W/m² reaches space, a difference of 159 W/m². Put another way, 40% of the longwave radiation leaving the surface never reaches space.

paragraphs.heading: Not quite like a greenhouse
paragraphs.text: The name comes from a comparison with greenhouses. Both keep in heat from sunlight, but in different ways. A greenhouse mainly works by blocking convection, the movement of air. The greenhouse effect instead restricts how radiation passes through the air and slows the rate at which thermal radiation is sent out to space.

paragraphs.heading: Two centuries of discovery
paragraphs.text: Joseph Fourier proposed the effect, without naming it, as early as 1824, and Claude Pouillet strengthened the case in 1827 and 1838. In 1856 Eunice Newton Foote showed that the sun warms moist air more than dry air, and air with carbon dioxide more still. John Tyndall was the first to measure how gases absorb and emit infrared; from 1859 he showed the effect came from a very small part of the atmosphere, mostly water vapor, though small amounts of hydrocarbons and carbon dioxide also mattered. Svante Arrhenius quantified it more fully in 1896, making the first numerical prediction of warming from a doubling of carbon dioxide. Nils Gustaf Ekholm first called it a greenhouse in 1901.

paragraphs.heading: The human push
paragraphs.text: Burning fossil fuels has added carbon dioxide and methane on top of the greenhouse gases already present in nature. Strengthening the natural effect with gases from human activity is called the enhanced greenhouse effect. By 2023 the result was about 1.2 °C of global warming since the Industrial Revolution, with the average surface temperature rising 0.18 °C per decade since 1981.
